{{Short description|Philosophical paradox regarding free will}}
{{about||the TV episode|Buridan's Ass (Fargo)}}
[[File:Deliberations of Congress.jpg|thumb|Political cartoon c.&nbsp;1900, showing the [[United States Congress]] as Buridan's ass (in the two hay piles version), hesitating between a [[Panama Canal|Panama route]] or a [[Nicaragua Canal|Nicaragua route]] for an [[History of the Panama Canal|Atlantic–Pacific canal]]]]

'''Buridan's ass''' is an illustration of a [[paradox]] in [[philosophy]] in the conception of [[free will]].<ref name="Clark">{{cite book
  | last = Clark
  | first = Michael 
  | title = Paradoxes from A to Z
  | publisher = Taylor and Francis
  | date = 2002
  | location = 
  | pages = 26-27
  | language = 
  | url = https://www.google.com/books/edition/Paradoxes_from_A_to_Z/aKyCAgAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1
  | archive-url= 
  | archive-date=
  | doi = 
  | id = 
  | isbn = 9781134586424
  | mr = 
  | zbl = 
  | jfm =}}</ref><ref name="Collyns">{{cite book
  | last = Collyns
  | first =  Kate 
  | title = Philosophy for Gardeners
  | publisher = Francis Lincoln
  | date = 2022
  | location = 
  | pages = 136
  | language = 
  | url = https://www.google.com/books/edition/Philosophy_for_Gardeners/wB9dEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22buridan%27s+ass%22+paradox
  | archive-url= 
  | archive-date=
  | doi = 
  | id = 
  | isbn = 9780711268210
  | mr = 
  | zbl = 
  | jfm =}}</ref> It refers to a hypothetical situation wherein an [[asinus|ass]] (or [[donkey]]) that is equally hungry and thirsty is placed precisely midway between a stack of [[hay]] and a pail of water. Since the paradox assumes the ass will always go to whichever is closer, it dies of both hunger and thirst since it cannot make any rational decision between the hay and water.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/doc/1O214-Buridansass.html |title=Buridan's ass: Oxford Companion to Phrase and Fable |publisher=Encyclopedia.com |access-date=2009-12-15}}</ref> A common variant of the paradox substitutes the hay and water for two identical piles of hay; the ass, unable to choose between the two, dies of hunger.

The paradox is named after the 14th-century [[France|French]] [[philosopher]] [[Jean Buridan]], whose philosophy of moral [[determinism]] it satirizes. 
Although the illustration is named after Buridan, philosophers have discussed the concept before him, notably [[Aristotle]], who put forward the example of a man equally hungry and thirsty,<ref name="Aristotle" >{{cite web |url=http://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/heavens.2.ii.html |title=On The Heavens (De Caelo), Book 2 Part 13.III |author=Aristotle, translated by J. L. Stocks |website=Internet Classics Archive|access-date=16 April 2024}}
</ref> and [[Al-Ghazali]], who used a man faced with the choice of equally good [[date (fruit)|dates]].<ref name=Kane/>

A version of this situation appears as [[Metastability (electronics)|metastability]] in [[digital electronics]], when an electric circuit must decide between two states based on an input that is in itself undefined (neither zero nor one). Metastability becomes a problem if the circuit spends more time than it should in this "undecided" state, which is usually set by the speed of the clock the system is using.

==History==
The paradox is found in [[Aristotle]]'s ''[[On the Heavens]]''.<ref name="Aristotle" /><ref name="Rescher">{{cite book
 | last = Rescher
 | first = Nicholas
 | title = Cosmos and Logos: Studies in Greek Philosophy
 | publisher = Walter de Gruyter
 | date = 2013
 | pages = 93–99
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=d-erjyNt2iAC
 | isbn = 978-3937202655
}}</ref> Aristotle, in ridiculing [[Anaximander]]'s idea that the Earth is stationary simply because it is spherical and any forces on it must be equal in all directions,<ref name="Vardoulakis" />{{rp|p.67}} says that is as ridiculous as saying that<ref name="Rescher" />
{{Quotation|...&nbsp;a man, being just as hungry as thirsty, and placed in between food and drink, must necessarily remain where he is and starve to death.|Aristotle, ''On the Heavens'' 295b, c. 350 BC }}
However, the Greeks only used this paradox as an analogy in the context of the equilibrium of ''physical'' forces.<ref name="Rescher" /> The 12th-century Persian scholar and philosopher [[Al-Ghazali]] discusses the application of this paradox to human decision making, asking whether it is possible to make a choice between equally good courses without grounds for preference.<ref name="Rescher" /> He takes the attitude that free will can break the stalemate.
{{Quotation|Suppose two similar dates in front of a man, who has a strong desire for them but who is unable to take them both. Surely he will take one of them, through a quality in him, the nature of which is to differentiate between two similar things.|[[Al-Ghazali|Abu Hamid al-Ghazali]], ''[[The Incoherence of the Philosophers]]'', c.  1100<ref name=Kane>{{cite book |last=Kane |first=Robert |title=A Contemporary Introduction to Free Will |year=2005 |publisher=Oxford |location=New York|pages=37}}</ref>}}

Andalusian philosopher [[Averroes]] (1126–1198), in commentary on Ghazali, takes the opposite view.<ref name="Rescher" /> 

Although Buridan nowhere discusses this specific problem,<ref name="Vardoulakis" />{{rp|p.67}} its relevance is that he did advocate a moral determinism whereby, save for ignorance or impediment, a human faced by alternative courses of action must always choose the greater [[good]]. In the face of equally good alternatives Buridan believed a rational choice could not be made.<ref name="Kinniment">{{cite book     | last = Kinniment  | first = David J.   | title = Synchronization and Arbitration in Digital Systems  | publisher = John Wiley & Sons  | date = 2008  | pages = 3  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_1p-BA4yriIC&pg=PA3
  | isbn = 978-0470517130}}</ref><ref name="SEP">{{cite web
  | last = Zupko
  | first = Frank 
  | title = John Buridan
  | work = Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
  | website = 
  | publisher = Dept. of Philosophy, Stanford University
  | date = 2024
  | url = https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/buridan/
  | format = 
  | doi = 
  | issn = 1095-5054
  | accessdate = 21 May 2025}}</ref>
{{Quotation|Should two courses be judged equal, then the will cannot break the deadlock, all it can do is to suspend judgement until the circumstances change, and the right course of action is clear.|Jean Buridan, c. 1340}} 
Later writers satirised this view in terms of an ass which, confronted by both food and water, must necessarily die of both hunger and thirst while pondering a decision.

Many later philosophers have addressed this problem of "choice without preference". In his ''[[Ethics (Spinoza book)|Ethics]]'' ({{circa|1661}}), [[Baruch de Spinoza]] accepts that his determinist philosophy implies that such a state of indecision could happen, but that this should be classed with other irrational behavior:<ref name="Vardoulakis">Clemens, Justin, "Spinoza's Ass", in {{cite book
  | last = Vardoulakis
  | first = Demitris
  | title = Spinoza Now
  | publisher = University of Minnesota Press
  | date = 2011
  | location = 
  | pages = 
  | language = 
  | url = https://www.google.com/books/edition/Spinoza_Now/naBlCKjmKfsC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=%22buridan%27s%20ass%22%20paradox
  | archive-url= 
  | archive-date=
  | doi = 
  | id = 
  | isbn = 9780816672806
  | mr = 
  | zbl = 
  | jfm =}}</ref>{{rp|p.71}}<ref name="Rescher" /> {{Quotation|[I]t may be objected, if man does not act from free will, what will happen if the incentives to action are equally balanced, as in the case of Buridan's ass? [In reply,] I am quite ready to admit, that a man placed in the equilibrium described (namely, as perceiving nothing but hunger and thirst, a certain food and a certain drink, each equally distant from him) would die of hunger and thirst. If I am asked, whether such a one should not rather be considered an ass than a man; I answer, that I do not know, neither do I know how a man should be considered, who hangs himself, or how we should consider children, fools, madmen, &c.|[[Baruch Spinoza]]|[[Ethics (Spinoza book)|Ethics]], book&nbsp;2, proposition 49, [[scholium]]}}
[[Pierre Bayle]] (1647–1706) in his ''Dictionnaire'' authored some of the most comprehensive discussions of the problem. He recognized explicitly that if humans have the ability to make a decision between choices with no reason for preference, this means that humans have [[free will]], and bears on man's rationalization of God's choices.  He regarded the previous examples of the ass or dates as artificial, and pointed out there are many real instances in everyday life in which a person must make a choice in which the choice doesn't matter to him, and that this presents no problem.<ref name="Rescher" />

[[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] (1646–1716) believed, from his [[principle of sufficient reason]], that if a person's preferences were really balanced no decision could be made, but that ''petites perceptions'', small perceived preferences below the threshold of consciousness that are always present, explain why people are able to make such a choice.<ref name="Rescher" />

==Discussion==
Some proponents of [[hard determinism]] such as Spinoza have granted the unpleasantness of the scenario, but have denied that it illustrates a true [[paradox]], since one does not [[contradiction|contradict]] oneself in suggesting that a man might die between two equally plausible routes of action. 

Other writers{{who|date=September 2014}} have opted to deny the validity of the illustration. A typical{{citation needed|date=September 2014}} counter-argument is that [[rationality]] as described in the paradox is so limited as to be a [[straw man]] version of the real thing, which does allow the consideration of meta-arguments. In other words, it is entirely rational to recognize that both choices are equally good and arbitrarily ([[randomness|randomly]]) pick one instead of starving; although the decision that they are sufficiently the same is also subject to Buridan's ass. The idea that a random decision could be made is sometimes used as an attempted justification for [[faith]] or intuitivity (called by Aristotle noetic or [[wikt:noesis|noesis]]). The argument is that, like the starving ass, we must make a choice to avoid being frozen in endless doubt. Other counter-arguments exist.{{specify|date=August 2014}}

According to Edward Lauzinger, Buridan's ass fails to incorporate the latent biases that humans always bring with them when making decisions.<ref>"Thought and Process", Lauzinger, Edward, 1994</ref>{{full|date=July 2013}}

Social psychologist Kurt Lewin's [[Field theory (psychology)|field theory]] treated this paradox experimentally.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03393765|title=On the Origin of Conflict Types|first=Noel W.|last=Smith|date=Apr 1, 1968|journal=The Psychological Record|volume=18|issue=2|pages=229–232|accessdate=May 15, 2023|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/BF03393765|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He demonstrated that lab rats experience difficulty when choosing between two equally attractive (approach–approach) goals. The typical response to approach–approach decisions is initial ambivalence, though the decision becomes more decisive as the organism moves towards one choice and away from another.

==Buridan's principle==
The situation of Buridan's ass was given a mathematical basis in a 1984 paper by American computer scientist [[Leslie Lamport]], in which Lamport presents an argument that, given certain assumptions about [[continuous function|continuity]] in a simple [[mathematical model]] of the Buridan's ass problem, there is always some starting condition under which the ass starves to death, no matter what strategy it takes.<ref name="Lamport">{{cite journal
  | last = Lamport
  | first = Leslie 
  | author-link = 
  | title = Buridan's principle
  | journal = Foundations of Physics
  | volume = 42
  | issue = 8
  | pages = 1056-1066
  | publisher = Springer
  | location = 
  | date = 2012
  | language = 
  | url = https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10701-012-9647-7
  | jstor = 
  | issn = 
  | doi = 10.1007/s10701-012-9647-7
  | id = 
  | mr = 
  | zbl = 
  | jfm = 
  | access-date = 21 May 2025| url-access = subscription
  }} Original December 1984 version published by Digital Equipment Corp  [http://research.microsoft.com/users/lamport/pubs/buridan.pdf archived here]</ref> He further illustrates the paradox with the example of a driver stopped at a [[railroad crossing]] trying to decide whether he has time to cross before a train arrives.  He proves that regardless of how "safe" the policy the driver adopts, because indecision can cause an indefinite delay in action, a small percentage of drivers will be hit by the train.

Lamport calls this result "Buridan’s principle":<ref name="Lamport" />
:A discrete decision based upon an input having a continuous range of values cannot be made within a bounded length of time.

He points out that just because we do not see asses or people starving to death through indecision, or other examples of Buridan's undecided states in real life, does not disprove the principle.  The persistence of a Buridan's undecided state for a perceptible length of time may just be sufficiently improbable that it has not been observed.

==Application to digital logic: metastability==
{{main|Metastability in electronics}}
A version of Buridan's principle occurs in [[electrical engineering]].<ref name="Lamport" /><ref name="Xanthopoulos">{{cite book
 | last1  = Xanthopoulos
 | first1 = Thucydides 
 | title  = Clocking in Modern VLSI Systems
 | publisher = Springer Science & Business Media
 | date   = 2009
 | pages  = 191
 | url    = https://books.google.com/books?id=UZZGAAAAQBAJ&q=buridan&pg=PA191
 | isbn   = 978-1441902610
 }}</ref><ref name="Niederman">{{cite book
 | last1  = Niederman
 | first1 = Derrick 
 | title  = The Puzzler's Dilemma
 | publisher = Penguin
 | date   = 2012
 | pages  = 130
 | url    = https://books.google.com/books?id=RvhGaqZ_oNUC&q=%22buridan%27s+ass%22&pg=PT130
 | isbn   = 978-1101560877
 }}</ref><ref name="Zbilut">{{cite book
 | last1  =  Zbilut
 | first1 = Joseph P.
 | title  = Unstable Singularities and Randomness
 | publisher = Elsevier
 | date   = 2004
 | pages  = 7
 | url    = https://books.google.com/books?id=YVid9QybwbUC&q=%22buridan%27s+ass%22+computer&pg=PA7
 | isbn   = 0080474691
 }}</ref><ref name="Kinniment2">{{cite book
 | last1  = Kinniment
 | first1 = David J. 
 | title  = Synchronization and Arbitration in Digital Systems
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 | date   = 2008
 | pages  = 2–6
 | url    = https://books.google.com/books?id=_1p-BA4yriIC&q=%22buridan%27s+ass%22&pg=PA2
 | isbn   = 978-0470517130
 }}</ref> Specifically, the input to a [[digital logic]] gate must convert a continuous [[voltage]] value into either a 0 or a 1, which is typically sampled and then processed. If the input is changing and at an intermediate value when sampled, the input stage acts like a [[comparator]]. The voltage value can then be likened to the position of the ass, and the values 0 and 1 represent the bales of hay. As in the situation of the starving ass, there exists an input on which the converter cannot make a proper decision, and the output remains balanced in a [[Metastability in electronics|metastable]] state between the two stable states for an undetermined length of time, until random noise in the circuit makes it converge to one of the stable states.

The metastability problem is a significant issue in [[digital circuit design]], and metastable states are a possibility wherever [[asynchronous circuit|asynchronous]] inputs (digital signals not synchronized to a [[clock signal]]) occur. The ultimate reason the problem is manageable is that the probability of a metastable state persisting longer than a given time interval ''t'' is an exponentially declining function of ''t''. In electronic devices, the probability of such an "undecided" state lasting longer than a matter of nanoseconds, while always possible, can be made negligibly low.

In [[asynchronous system|asynchronous system design]], [[Arbiter (electronics)|arbiter circuits]] have been developed to make such decisions. They can reduce to insignificance the probability that a metastable state occurs, at the cost of increased decision time.<ref name=arbiter>{{cite journal
|last1       =Sutherland
|first1      =Ivan E.
|author-link1 =Ivan Sutherland
|last2       =Ebergen
|first2      =Jo
|title       =Computers Without Clocks
|journal     =[[Scientific American]]
|volume      =287
|issue       =2
|date        =August 2002
|pages       =62–69
|doi =10.1038/scientificamerican0802-62
|pmid =12140955
|bibcode =2002SciAm.287b..62S
}}</ref>
